theme: seal text identity, locality of duplicates and sealing matches
question: Do identical Indus seal texts behave like personal names (duplicates local to one city) or like labels used across cities, and what do whole-text reuse, motif concordance and sealing-seal matches add?
outcome: 1,430 complete single-line seals from named South Asian sites; 65 texts recur on 174 seals, 41 at more than one site. Frozen test: same-site share of duplicate pairs 0.473 against 0.448 (p 0.31, ratio 1.06). Length-stratified null: 0.473 against 0.382 (p 0.032). Post-review breakdown: Mohenjo-daro duplicates at chance (59 against 60.2 same-site pairs), Harappa 10 against 6.0, other sites 7 against 1.5 (p 0.002); about 15% of shared texts wholly local, compatible up to 25%. Identical pairs of four or more signs exceed a bigram model 3.1- to 5.3-fold; none among 445 seals of six or more signs. Motif concordance comes from unicorn pairs (88 of 89 matches); 1 of 42 pairs with another animal matches. Of 16 sealings matching seals (6 texts), 13 (4 texts) match only seals elsewhere, including Lothal L-161 to L-170 with the four-sign text of Mohenjo-daro fragment M-895.
challenge: Mohenjo-daro supplies 917 of 1,430 seals; the site breakdown is post hoc with small counts; motif codes come from catalogues and M-895 is a fragment; common names would also spread across cities.
remedy: Frozen protocol; exact hypergeometric and enumeration checks; length-stratified and variant-merged sensitivities; adversarial review with recomputed checks (Amendment 3).
retry_when: Plate-checked motifs and texts for L-161 and M-895, dated contexts for duplicate seals, or an object-level seal corpus of a known script allow a calibrated comparison.
